title: Selling Professional Services on AWS Marketplace
summary: Selling professional services on AWS Marketplace: what qualifies, how services listings differ from SaaS, private offers for services, and use cases.
body_text: A professional services listing on AWS Marketplace is an offering for human-delivered work — assessments, implementation, training, or managed services — scoped and priced per engagement and transacted through a private offer, rather than provisioned self-serve like a SaaS or AMI product. Most people picture AWS Marketplace as a catalog of software you subscribe to and provision yourself. That’s most of it — but it isn’t all of it. The same marketplace that sells a SaaS contract can also sell the implementation project, the migration, the training program, and the managed service that surrounds it. For ISVs and consulting partners, that opens a second motion: the work you already deliver off-platform can be transacted on the marketplace your customer already buys software through, against the cloud budget they’ve already committed to spend. Here’s how professional services listings work, how they differ from software, and when they’re worth the effort. What a professional services listing is A professional services listing is a marketplace offering for human-delivered work rather than software a buyer provisions themselves. It covers the engagements that surround a software purchase, and it’s transacted through the marketplace’s billing and agreement rails instead of a separate contract and invoice. Services listings generally fall into four categories: Assessments : Scoped diagnostic engagements — a readiness review, an architecture assessment, a security or cost audit — that produce findings and a recommendation. Implementation and professional services : Deployment, configuration, integration and migration work that stands up a product or platform for the customer. Training and enablement : Structured programs that get a customer’s team productive on a product or technology. Managed and support services : Ongoing operation, monitoring or support delivered on a recurring basis rather than a one-time project. Each is quote-based and scoped to a specific customer. That single fact is what makes services listings behave differently from everything else in the catalog. How professional services differ from SaaS and AMI listings Professional services listings differ from SaaS or AMI listings in one structural way: they are custom-scoped and quote-based, so they’re delivered through a private offer rather than a self-serve public price. A buyer can’t click “subscribe” on a migration — the scope, timeline and price are negotiated first, then transacted. That difference cascades into how the listing is built, priced and fulfilled. Professional services listing SaaS / AMI listing What’s sold Human-delivered work — a project, program or ongoing service Software the buyer provisions and runs themselves Pricing Custom, per-engagement, quote-based Public price, or private offer on top of it Purchase path Private offer, negotiated then accepted Self-serve subscribe, or private offer Fulfillment Delivered by the seller off-platform; the marketplace handles billing and agreement Provisioned automatically through the platform Metering Fixed scope or milestone-based Usage- or subscription-metered The through-line: software is productized and self-serve; services are scoped and quote-based. The marketplace gives both the same billing, agreement and procurement rails — the fulfillment is what differs. Who can list professional services Two kinds of sellers list professional services: consulting and services partners whose core business is delivery, and ISVs that bundle services around their own software. Eligibility runs through the AWS seller and partner programs, and services listings sit alongside your other offerings once you’re registered to sell. For a consulting partner, the services listing is the product — the assessment, the migration, the managed service is what the customer is buying. For an ISV, services are usually the layer that makes the software succeed: the implementation that gets a buyer live, or the managed service that keeps them there. Both list through the same marketplace mechanics covered in our guide to AWS Marketplace for sellers , and both benefit from the same billing and procurement rails as software. The difference is only what gets delivered after the offer is accepted. How buyers purchase professional services Buyers purchase professional services through a private offer: the seller scopes the engagement, sends a custom offer with the agreed price and terms, and the buyer accepts it through their AWS account. From that point the transaction behaves like any other marketplace purchase — it’s billed through AWS and appears on the customer’s consolidated cloud bill. The reason this matters is the budget it draws against. Because the engagement transacts through AWS, it can count toward the customer’s committed cloud spend — including drawdown against an Enterprise Discount Program (EDP) commitment. A buyer with a large multi-year AWS commitment can apply your services engagement toward that number instead of finding fresh budget, which is often the difference between a project that gets approved this quarter and one that waits. Setting this up is the same workflow as software: you build the offering as one of your marketplace listings , then extend private offers for services to named buyers with the scope and price you negotiated. Use cases for services listings The strongest use cases pair a services listing with something the customer is already buying or committed to: Bundle implementation with your software : Sell the SaaS subscription and the deployment project as one marketplace transaction, so the buyer procures the outcome — software that’s live — not just the license. Migrations and modernization : Transact a cloud migration or re-platforming engagement against the customer’s AWS commitment, where the work and the resulting usage land on the same bill. Managed services : Offer ongoing operation or support as a recurring services engagement, giving the customer a single marketplace relationship for both the software and the team that runs it. Training and enablement : Attach a structured onboarding or certification program to a software deal so adoption is procured, not left to chance. In each case, the services listing removes a second procurement cycle. The customer signs once, through a vendor they’ve already onboarded. Benefits of routing services through the marketplace Routing professional services through AWS Marketplace gives you three things a separate contract can’t: access to committed cloud budget, a procurement path the customer has already approved, and consolidated billing that puts your engagement on the same invoice as their software. Together they shorten the path from scoped to signed. For the buyer, the engagement draws on budget they’ve already set aside and clears procurement they’ve already run — no new vendor onboarding, no fresh purchase order. For the seller, the deal moves at marketplace speed instead of legal-and-invoicing speed, and it strengthens the same AWS Marketplace relationship your software already runs through. The services aren’t a separate business; they’re the same customer, transacted the same way. Frequently asked questions Can you sell professional services on AWS Marketplace? Yes. AWS Marketplace supports professional services listings for assessments, implementation, training, and managed or support services. Unlike software, these are custom-scoped and quote-based, so they’re transacted through a private offer the buyer accepts rather than a self-serve subscription. How is a services listing different from a SaaS listing? A SaaS listing sells software the buyer provisions themselves at a public or negotiated price. A services listing sells human-delivered work — scoped, quoted, and delivered by the seller off-platform. Both are billed through the marketplace, but only software is self-serve. Do professional services count toward committed cloud spend? They can. Because the engagement transacts through AWS, it can draw down against the customer’s committed spend, including an Enterprise Discount Program (EDP) commitment. That’s often why buyers prefer to procure services through the marketplace rather than a separate contract. How do buyers purchase professional services? Through a private offer. The seller scopes the engagement and sends a custom offer with agreed price and terms; the buyer accepts it through their AWS account. It then bills through AWS and appears on the customer’s consolidated cloud bill. Can ISVs bundle services with their software? Yes. An ISV can sell a software subscription and its implementation, migration or managed service as marketplace transactions to the same buyer — so the customer procures a working outcome, not just a license, through one already-approved vendor relationship. Takeaways Professional services listings sell human-delivered work — assessments, implementation, training, managed services — not software the buyer provisions themselves. They’re custom-scoped and quote-based, so they transact through a private offer, not a self-serve subscribe. Because the engagement bills through AWS, it can draw down committed cloud spend, including EDP commitments. The strongest plays bundle a services listing with software the customer is already buying, removing a second procurement cycle. Suger runs professional services listings on the same platform that manages your marketplace listings, private offers and billing across AWS and other clouds. See how it fits your services motion on the AWS Marketplace solution page.

title: Universal Managed Agents
summary: One API to run agents across eight harnesses and any model, in Modal, Daytona, or E2B sandboxes — configured at creation with the open Universal Agent Protocol.
body_text: Today we're introducing Universal Managed Agents: a single API to deploy agents across 8+ harnesses, including Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode, without managing infrastructure or credentials. One request creates an agent, provisions it a computer, and puts it to work: Request · POST /v2/threads bash curl https://api.brainbaselabs.com/v2/threads \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $BRAINBASE_API_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d ' { "agent" : { "harness" : "claude_code" , "model" : "claude-sonnet-5" , "instructions" : "You are a concise research assistant." }, "input" : "In two sentences, what is MCP?" } ' Response · 201 Created json { "thread_id" : "a4fe9c41-7fea-4b93-91e4-081329e35865" , "agent_id" : "54850f1a-e68f-46ac-a85c-01f977101f91" , "status" : "running" } The response returns before the agent finishes. From that point on you are talking to a running colleague: poll the thread, append messages, or subscribe to a live event stream of everything it does. Universal Managed Agents expands on Anthropic's Claude Managed Agents, which pairs Claude with an Anthropic-run agent loop and sandbox. We think that shape — agents as a managed resource rather than a pile of infrastructure — is right. Universal Managed Agents generalizes it to any model, any harness, and any sandbox provider. Agents are customized at creation using the open-source Universal Agent Protocol (UAP) : one spec that declares instructions, MCP servers, skills, permissions, and secrets, independent of the harness that will run them. Once created, agents live in secure sandboxes with their own computers, and you can message them for as long as the thread lives. # Supported models and harnesses A harness is the runtime an agent works inside: how it receives work, touches files, runs commands, and reports progress. Universal Managed Agents launches with eight, all behind the same request shape — the same payload, the same response, switched with a single harness field. Harness API value Built for Kafka kafka_cloud Production knowledge work, surfaces, and orchestrations Claude Code claude_code Codebase-focused work and developer iteration Codex codex Code implementation, review, and workspace tasks Cursor cursor Agentic coding on Cursor's runtime Factory Droid factory End-to-end software engineering tasks OpenCode opencode Open-source coding agent workflows Qoder qoder Coding tasks on Qoder's agentic runtime Qwen Code qwen Coding workflows on Qwen models Models are just as interchangeable. Pass any model ID as the model field: GPT-5.6 Sol, Terra, and Luna from OpenAI, Claude Opus 4.8 and Sonnet 5 from Anthropic, Gemini 3.5 Flash from Google, Grok 4.5 from xAI, and open-weights models like GLM 5.2, DeepSeek V4, and Kimi K2.7 Code served through Baseten. Because the model and the harness are independent fields, pairings that used to take an integration — Kimi inside OpenCode, Gemini inside Codex — are now a one-line change. # Example agents The fastest way to get a feel for the API is to read a few requests. Give an engineering agent a red test suite and a warm sandbox. Its entrypoint prepares the repository before the first turn; the agent runs the tests, fixes the defect, and keeps iterating until the suite is green: Fix a failing test suite json { "agent" : { "harness" : "claude_code" , "model" : "claude-sonnet-5" , "instructions" : "Turn failing test suites green without changing test files." , "entrypoint" : "git clone $REPOSITORY_URL /workspace/app && cd /workspace/app && pip install -e '.[test]'" }, "input" : "Run pytest in /workspace/app, fix the defect, and verify the full suite passes." } A product agent can build a small web app, start its server, and leave it running in the sandbox. Resolve port 3000 through the machine preview API and the result is live immediately, with no deployment step: Ship a live app json { "agent" : { "harness" : "claude_code" , "model" : "claude-sonnet-5" , "instructions" : "Build small web apps and keep their server running." }, "input" : "Build a single-page TODO app, then serve it on 0.0.0.0:3000 in the background. Leave the server running." } To compare harnesses on your own work, send the same task to several agents in parallel. Each gets an isolated sandbox; when they finish, download the same output file from every thread and grade the results against one hidden test suite: One task, four harnesses json [ { "agent" : { "harness" : "claude_code" }, "input" : "Fix search() in solution.py. Write the final implementation to solution.py." }, { "agent" : { "harness" : "codex" }, "input" : "Fix search() in solution.py. Write the final implementation to solution.py." }, { "agent" : { "harness" : "cursor" }, "input" : "Fix search() in solution.py. Write the final implementation to solution.py." }, { "agent" : { "harness" : "opencode" }, "input" : "Fix search() in solution.py. Write the final implementation to solution.py." } ] These are three real patterns built from the same primitives: create a thread, let the agent work in its sandbox, then continue the thread or inspect its machine. Follow-up messages reuse the warm sandbox, every turn is available over a live SSE event stream, and file operations let you pull artifacts back out. The full surface is documented at docs.brainbaselabs.com/api . # Architecture When a request arrives, the UAP spec is normalized and content-addressed: identical specs resolve to the same agent_id , so retries and fan-outs never mint duplicate agents. The control plane then provisions a machine with your chosen sandbox provider, translates the spec into the target harness's native configuration, and starts the run. Your application POST /v2/threads Universal API UAP agent spec · content-addressed agents · threads, messages, events Harness adapters kafka_cloud claude_code codex cursor factory opencode qoder qwen Sandbox providers modal daytona e2b One request shape in; any harness, any model, any sandbox underneath. Everything after creation hangs off the thread. A thread carries the transcript, the event log, and the machine. Its status moves through running , success , fail , need_more_info , and idle — an agent that needs a decision from you parks itself instead of guessing. Files move in and out of the agent's machine through a files API, and long-lived agents can share a mounted folder across threads. # Comparison to Claude Managed Agents Claude Managed Agents got the managed-agent shape right: persisted agent configs, server-run sessions, skills and MCP, secrets that never touch your client. Universal Managed Agents keeps that shape and removes the constraints on what runs inside it. Universal Managed Agents Claude Managed Agents Models Configurable: Any provider — OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, xAI, plus open-weights models via Baseten Fixed: Claude models Harnesses Configurable: Eight at launch: Kafka, Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Factory Droid, OpenCode, Qoder, Qwen Code Fixed: Anthropic's Claude harness Sandboxes Configurable: Modal, Daytona, and E2B, natively Fixed: Anthropic-hosted containers, or self-hosted Configuration Configurable: One UAP spec: instructions, MCP servers, skills, secrets, entrypoint Configurable: Agent objects: system prompt, MCP servers, skills, tools, permission policies Conversations Configurable: Threads with messages and an SSE event stream Configurable: Sessions with messages and an SSE event stream Secrets Configurable: Planted into the sandbox environment at creation Configurable: Vault credentials substituted at egress Agent identity Configurable: Content-addressed — the same spec is the same agent Configurable: Versioned configs — sessions pin a version Configurable — pick any option, per agent Fixed — one vendor-decided option If you're already on Claude Managed Agents, the mental model carries over almost one-to-one: agents map to agents, sessions to threads, environments to machines. The difference is that each layer is now a field you can change. # Sandboxes Universal Managed Agents has native support for Modal, Daytona, and E2B sandboxes. Every thread runs on its own machine — a real computer with a filesystem, a shell, and network access — never on shared infrastructure, and never on yours. The provider is one more field. Set machine_kind on the agent, override the base image per provider with a snapshot , and use entrypoint to install dependencies before the first turn. Machines are first-class API objects too, with their own lifecycle, status, and preview endpoints: POST /v2/machines bash curl https://api.brainbaselabs.com/v2/machines \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $BRAINBASE_API_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d ' { "kind" : "daytona" , "agent_id" : "54850f1a-e68f-46ac-a85c-01f977101f91" , "snapshot" : "python-3.12-playwright" } ' Universal Managed Agents is available today for every Brainbase workspace. Start at app.brainbaselabs.com , or create your first thread straight from the API docs . Managed agents made agents feel like a resource instead of a project. Universal Managed Agents makes that resource universal.

title: How Darryl Cuttell’s Would-Be IHRA Empire Came Crashing Down
summary: If we define “failure” for a long-struggling drag racing series as passing ownership of said series along to somebody else because you no longer want to deal with it, here’s the shorthand for the 56-year history of the International Hot Rod Association: Fail. Fail. Fail. Fail. Fail. Fail. Fail. Fail. Fail. Fail. We boldfaced that […]
body_text: If we define “failure” for a long-struggling drag racing series as passing ownership of said series along to somebody else because you no longer want to deal with it, here’s the shorthand for the 56-year history of the International Hot Rod Association: Fail. Fail. Fail. Fail. Fail. Fail. Fail. Fail. Fail. Fail. We boldfaced that last fail because that’s the one going on now, and it dwarfs the rest. Ten owners, 10 attempts to elevate the second-tier IHRA to racing relevancy that might possibly rival the dominant, 75-year-old National Hot Rod Association (NHRA): The current unpleasantness is the most sport-shattering misfire of them all, as the IHRA’s current owner is blaming, by name, the richest man in the world. Really? Elon Musk is responsible for the collapse of IHRA drag racing? So says Darryl Cuttell, 61, who bought the IHRA in December of 2024. IHRA owner Darryl Cuttell (R) with recently appointed (May 2026) president Dustin Farthing. Facebook/IHRA Cuttell, himself a master electrician, is the owner of 30-year-old Darana Hybrid, an Ohio company that describes itself as, “a Native American owned and operated international electro-mechanical contractor,” an acknowledgement of Cuttell’s membership in the Tuscarora Nation. In 2024, Darana Hybrid was the lead contractor on Musk’s new data center in Memphis, Tennessee, which Musk calls his “Colossus.” Musk wanted contractors who would complete Colossus now —he needed massive computing capacity to train the company’s Grok large language models. Most contractors said Musk’s timeline was impossible, but Cuttell and Darana Hybrid signed on. Elon Musk and his company, xAI, say that Colossus was completed in just 122 days. Cuttell says 123. It is not the only thing Musk and Cuttell disagree on. The $1.25-trillion merger earlier this year between Musk’s Space X and xAI, Cuttell said, was when the problems began. xAI promptly paid the invoices Darana Hybrid sent in. Space xAI, now the curator of Colossus and its data-center siblings, hasn’t. Musk’s properties, including Tesla and The Boring Company, have earned a slow-pay reputation that may or may not be warranted. “It’s what Elon does. He goes out and takes on the small guys and just buries them,” Cuttell told WMC, the Memphis NBC affiliate. “I’ve never been treated so unfair for doing such a good job. That’s the worst part. I overextended myself, gave him everything he wanted, and now I’m getting trashed.” So Cuttell filed liens with the county for unpaid work for Musk on two data centers totaling $136,892,782.78, and he plans to file liens for $400 million more. Cuttell told a Memphis newspaper that Darana Hybrid has done $1.5 billion worth of work on Musk data centers, and Darana is still owed a substantial percentage of that. Typically, Musk and his companies ignore critics. Not this time. Last Thursday, Space xAI filed a federal suit against Darana Hybrid, and the 40-page complaint is just brutal. And if you were wondering what drag racing and the International Hot Rod Association had to do with all this, here it is: Along with Cuttell himself, the IHRA is actually named in the suit. That suit alleges that Darana and Cuttell overbilled Space xAI “by hundreds of millions of dollars while selling out their own suppliers and subcontractors along the way,” and “diverted money to Cuttell’s personal side projects,” which would be the IHRA, the dozen or so racetracks he bought both before and after that acquisition, and a peculiar list of other competitive sports leagues he purchased, including a snowmobile racing series, 10 classes of jetski racing, at least five truck and tractor pulling leagues, 32 classes of Inshore and Offshore boat racing, drag boating, Formula 1 boat racing, and finally, “rodeo and bull riding.” Almost overnight, the IHRA went from being almost out of business to sanctioning 137 different classes of competition. (There are dozens of IHRA “member” tracks, as well as dozens of NHRA member tracks. The tracks run IHRA or NHRA rules, and victories at the little tracks help decide regional championships.) Jared C. Tilton/Getty Images/NASCAR Among those sanctioning classes was an oval track stock car series which only lasted for a handful of races before the IHRA pulled the plug. That parallels one of Cuttell’s most puzzling purchases: Rockingham Speedway, the (almost) one-mile oval track in Rockingham, North Carolina, in the middle of NASCAR country. The 61-year-old track hosted NASCAR races up until 2004, and the track was closed for long periods until 2025, when NASCAR returned with its Craftsman Truck series and the O’Reilly Auto Parts series, and the track was angling to get a NASCAR Cup race. Given the turbulence around Cuttell and the IHRA, some industry insiders wonder if Rockingham will be hosting any NASCAR racing at all in 2027. For IHRA racers, Darryl Cuttell and his seemingly bottomless checking account was an answered prayer. In 2024, Cuttell came riding up on a white stallion to save the series—or more accurately, in a black, 1970 split-grille Chevrolet Camaro Pro Mod—which he had purchased from Larry Jeffers Race Cars, a dragster builder in House Springs, Missouri. It so happened that Jeffers was the latest owner of the IHRA, and it also happened that Cuttell had come into some money. Instagram/ihradragracing How much money? That’s unclear. But last week I spoke to Richard Freeman, owner of Elite Motorsports, which qualified seven cars into the Top Fuel and Pro Stock classes at the most recent NHRA race, the Northwest Nationals in Seattle. He also has several businesses back home in Oklahoma, not all of them racing-related. Freeman recently paid a visit to the secretive Cuttell at Darana Hybrid in Hamilton, Ohio. Cuttell wanted Freeman to buy the IHRA and become owner number eleven. The price: $500 million. According to Freeman, Cuttell told him, “Man, I’m in bad shape,” and more than once Cuttell complained that “Elon Musk owes me $600 million.” As mentioned, Cuttell said in an interview last Friday with a Memphis newspaper that Musk owes Darana Hybrid 40 percent of the $1.5 billion in work that he says he did for Musk on his data centers—which comes out to exactly $600 million. So assuming that Cuttell has already been paid said 60 percent of $1.5 billion, that would suggest that Cuttell has collected $900,000,000. Out of that, Cuttell had to pay salaries, expenses, and subcontractors, but apparently he had enough left over to turn the drag racing world on its head. Now, though, it sounds like there’s very little left of the money Cuttell was paid. He told the Daily Memphian that he owes $200 million to vendors and isn’t sure how he will pay them. Presumably that’s in addition to what he owes drag racers and support staff, as well as purses for the other non-drag racing series he bought, plus the notes and taxes due on his racetracks. As for Richard Freeman, he offered Cuttell $7 million for the IHRA’s rolling stock, which included multiple 18-wheelers and some tractors. Cuttell turned it down. “And that was that,” Freeman said. “No way was I interested in buying the series and those racetracks.” By most accounts, Cuttell did very little negotiating for the tracks he bought, often paying well over market value. Freeman said Cuttell bought the long-dormant Heartland Motorsports Park in Topeka, Kansas, for $40 million. “Two years ago,” Freeman said, “I could have bought that place for $6 million.” Facebook/IHRA Aside from possibly overpaying for the tracks and series he bought, Cuttell offered race purses that were far richer than the IHRA could ever pay, in any of its nine previous incarnations. In April, I wrote about this particular IHRA’s last gasp, the IHRA Triple Crown . Which turned out to be the Just-One Crown, as the last two legs were cancelled, and racers haven’t been paid for the first leg, with some owed six figures. The IHRA was offering comparatively enormous purses for the three Triple Crown races, all scheduled for off weekends for the rival NHRA, thinking some of the big names from that series would be attracted by the money; for Top Fuel and Funny Car, the three races would pay $150,000 for a win at each of the three tracks, more than double what the NHRA pays. And if a racer won all three Triple Crown races, they’d be paid an additional $1 million. The Triple Crown was to be held at three separate tracks—first at Darana Maple Grove Raceway in Pennsylvania, then Darana National Trail Raceway in Ohio, with the finale at Darana Memphis Motorsports Park. (Cuttell names all the tracks he buys “Darana,” which is rumored to be a portmanteau of Darryl’s first name and the first name of his sister, which may or may not be “Ana.”) Facebook/IHRA Darana Maple Grove is one of the IHRA’s best tracks; Cuttell bought it while the Performance Racing Industry show in Indianapolis was underway last December. The purchase was a stunner, and if it was meant to embarrass the NHRA, it did, because they had a big race scheduled at Maple Grove later this year. The following week, the NHRA yanked the race from Maple Grove and rescheduled it at US 131 Motorsports Park in Martin, Michigan, which has never hosted a major NHRA race. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Maple Grove Raceway (@maplegrove1320) The leadoff Triple Crown race at Maple Grove was rained out; it was rescheduled for Darana National Trail Raceway in Ohio. But none of the marquee NHRA racers showed up, just the IHRA regulars. The IHRA promptly cancelled the two remaining Triple Crown races, then cancelled almost everything else, except for some tractor pull events. For some reason, they found traction. Facebook/IHRA Up until then, the money Cuttell was spending was nothing short of astounding, much to the delight of the long-suffering, IHRA-faithful racers. Besides the big purses, he provided multiple perks for all of the competitors, their families and crew members, including free dinners and free deliveries of ice in the morning. Cuttell typically arrived in style, aboard a newly acquired helicopter or in the Darana Hybrid private jet, a Bombardier Challenger 300 with VIP seating. Once, he sent his jet to pick up drag racing pioneers “Big Daddy” Don Garlits , 94, and his longtime nemesis, Shirley Muldowney, 86, for a personal appearance at an IHRA track. Pro racers were impressed. Sportsman racers—those who do it primarily for love, not money—felt like they’d died and gone to heaven. By mid-season, they changed their tune and figured they’d only got it half right. Garlits says he is still owed the $5000 appearance fee he was promised. During this most recent decline, and amid the long list of warning signs, IHRA devotees were nevertheless stalwart in their love for Cuttell, roundly criticizing news outlets who reported the facts; bad news was the fault of those who printed it, and all. A much smaller contingent, though, saw black helicopters with every development, viewed every shred of information as an opportunity for a new and unsubstantiated theory of malfeasance. Leading that conjecture was an assertion that Cuttell was buying tracks to get the land, which he would eventually flip to Musk, who would replace the racing with data centers. That wasn’t remotely the truth. But nobody knew for sure, because Cuttell wasn’t talking, and he did not return phone calls for this story. I also reached out to NHRA director of PR and communications Josh Hachat, for his company’s thoughts on Cuttell and the IHRA, but he replied, “We’ll probably steer clear on commenting. We prefer focusing on our 75th anniversary.” Failed Promises Richard Freeman at left. Will Lester/MediaNews Group/Inland Valley Daily Bulletin/Getty Images Arguably, the biggest mistake Cuttell made with the IHRA was hiring, then promptly firing, some highly qualified motorsports executives. “You could see the writing on the wall, because anyone he hired, who had any sense at all, stayed there a very short time. And that’s because they weren’t ‘yes’ people. I don’t think his intentions were bad,” Freeman said, “but they were completely handled the wrong way.” Early on, I was sufficiently interested in Cuttell and his IHRA to write a story for Hagerty in April 2025 titled, “Does the Refreshed IHRA Mean a New Era in Drag Racing? We’ll Know Soon Enough.” It was based largely on a phone interview with the IHRA’s Alan Reinhart, who had spent three decades as an announcer with the powerhouse NHRA. I spoke to him on Monday, April 21, and the story ran the next day. In it, Reinhart spoke passionately about the IHRA in general, owner Darryl Cuttell in particular: “You look at his business background, and his philosophy is that failure is not an option. He’s very driven, he’s very dedicated to it, and we have the resources to make it happen. And that’s exactly what we’re going to do.” Six days later, I got an email from Reinhart. “Hey Steven, thanks for the nice story about the IHRA. If you haven’t heard, Rich Schaefer and I are no longer with the company. Not sure what their plan is now.” Schaefer, previously an NHRA division director, was named president of the IHRA less than three months before. He replaced Kenny Nowling, who lasted two weeks working for Cuttell. Also gone: Scott “Woody” Woodruff, the chief operating officer who is very well regarded in the industry, and who had become the de facto face of the IHRA, since Cuttell is profoundly camera-shy. Woodruff said he pointed out internally that the IHRA’s online registration portal was so difficult to use that some racers just give up halfway through. It was not well received. After nine months on the job, he was terminated with a one-word text from Cuttell: “Fired.” Woodruff’s response: “Thank you.” Seemingly, there was no one Cuttell trusted enough to take their advice. He bought Atlanta Dragway, which had been owned by the NHRA until it decided it didn’t want the track any longer, and the grandstands were subsequently removed and the tower razed. What Cuttell bought was basically Georgia prairie, interrupted by two remaining strips of pavement. Cuttell said he’d rebuild it, and there would be racing there by the end of the year. There will not be. Memphis Motorsports Park, renamed Darana Motorsports Park Millington. Facebook/IHRA Facebook/IHRA He also bought Memphis Motorsports Park, which, like Heartland Park in Topeka, has a drag strip, oval track and a road course. It has been abandoned for years, and much of what is left has been vandalized. Cuttell pledged $60 million for track improvements, and there would be racing there by the end of the year, the local chamber of commerce was told. There will not. Same thing with Heartland Park, though it is in far better shape than Memphis or Atlanta. The track was energized, and work was being done to bring the track back. There was even a manager overseeing it all, Emily Mawhinney, but she said on Facebook that she was fired by the IHRA, via email, in July. Amid the uncertainty, work has ceased, and several non-spectator events scheduled there have been cancelled. No one knows what will happen to the tracks Cuttell bought: Some were reportedly owner-financed and would likely go back to the previous owner. Cuttell indicated to the Memphis TV station that he would likely have to sell some properties to help pay his bills, but potential buyers may be wary. Facebook/IHRA Facebook/IHRA Darana Dragway-Milan Facebook/IHRA That visit to Darana Hybrid to look over inventory was not Richard Freeman’s first interaction with Cuttell. Two years ago, at a drag race, he listened in as Cuttell explained his business plan to other racers. Freeman was puzzled. “Nobody”, Freeman said last week, “who is a business guy, does something like that, because it makes zero sense. At any level, from any angle, zero sense.” As for Elite Top Fuel driver and three-time NASCAR champion Tony Stewart—who drives for Freeman but owns Tony Stewart Racing, which fields an NHRA Top Fuel car for his wife Leah Pruett and a Funny Car for Matt Hagan—it caps a year of frustration. He was at least interested in what Cuttell planned for the IHRA and wanted to hear him out, but Stewart said “I couldn’t get him on the phone. Not once. Not all year.” Top Fuel racer Tony Stewart celebrates with Elite Motorsports team owner Richard Freeman, and Elite Pro Stock driver Erica Enders, after winning the 66th annual NHRA Winternationals at In-N-Out Burger Pomona Dragstrip on April 12. Will Lester/MediaNews Group/Getty Images The Leah Martin reign Leah Martin Facebook/IHRA Between the date of Cuttell’s IHRA purchase and now, the organization had at least five presidents, or six, if you count a president who now insists that no, he was never actually president. One of Cuttell’s more interesting hires for president was Leah Martin, who ran a prestigious boat race at Lake of the Ozarks in Missouri. Cuttell likes fast boats, and he had acquired Spirit of Qatar , a Mystic catamaran powered by a pair of T55 turbine engines that had reportedly been boosted to a total of 7500 horsepower. Sheikh Hassan bin Jabor Al-Thani, along with throttleman Steve Curtis, had made a 244-mph run, a world record, at the Ozarks event in 2014. Spirit of Qatar was tuned up and rebranded the Darana Hybrid in the now-familiar chartreuse green that Cuttell favors on almost everything, be it his plant in Ohio, or his websites, or the buildings on his racetracks. At the 2024 Ozarks event, Cuttell and carryover throttleman Curtis made a 242-mph pass on a circuit that was a quarter-mile shorter than the one for the Sheikh’s 244-mph run. Though Martin had no drag racing experience, she apparently impressed Cuttell, and she was introduced as the IHRA president at the December 2025 PRI trade show, the first female president of any major motorsports sanctioning body. Five months later, Martin was overseeing the major Thunder on the Beach event in Cocoa Beach, Florida, part of the IHRA Offshore Series, one of the puzzling non-drag-racing series that Cuttell had either bought or begun. Cuttell had announced he would be pumping an incomprehensible $7.2 million into the Powerboat series, including a purse of $2 million. Facebook/IHRA Facebook/IHRA Facebook/IHRA Facebook/IHRA Facebook/IHRA In the middle of that Cocoa Beach event, with no discussion, Martin learned she was “let go in a very public way without an explanation I still haven’t received,” she wrote on LinkedIn. In a separate text, she wrote, “I’m at a loss for words, I have poured my heart and soul into this sport at the cost of time with my family.” IHRA According to the website speedonthewater.com , which covered the Cocoa race: “Martin’s husband, Justin, was the IHRA safety director. When he found out Leah had been fired right before the start of the Super V and Extreme race, he reportedly had the pace boat head back in to the pits and he disembarked. Because it’s about a 15-minute ride from the pits to the racecourse, that created a major delay to the start of the race.” One of the competitors inconvenienced “was IHRA president Darryl Cuttle (sic) who was racing unopposed” in a 52-foot MTI catamaran. That story also said that Utah insurance executive Tommy Thomassie, an experienced marine competition pro, had replaced Leah Martin, effective immediately. His presidential reign was brief. “Darryl asked me to take the position, I accepted it, and he personally told several people, introducing me as the president of the IHRA,” Thomassie told Hagerty. “The following day [May 18], I received a call from Dustin Farthing, who patched in Darryl, and Darryl then informed me that he had made a mistake; he intended for me to be president of Powerboating, and Dustin Farthing was going to the president of the IHRA. And all of this was weeks after I had resigned my position as executive vice-president and director of Powerboating.” Indeed, Cuttell had reached into his IHRA Professional Watercraft Series for the latest and reportedly still-current overall president, Dustin Farthing, a watercraft racer. In fact, according to his own website, Farthing “is thought by many to be the greatest Jet Ski racer of all time.” From outward appearances, it looks as though Farthing’s main responsibility has been to provide corporate quotes for press releases announcing the postponement and reorganization of the IHRA’s various series, with an exception being tractor pulling, which seems to have survived and is all that remains of the IHRA.com’s reporting on current events. Eleven of the last 12 stories in the “Latest News” section are about tractor pulls. Facebook/IHRA The Cuttell-Musk Connection As for the previously mentioned dealings between Darryl Cuttell and the world’s richest man, given the amount of time and energy and money Cuttell has spent on the IHRA these past two years, it seems possible that his dedication to the sport came at the expense of his core business, Darana Hybrid. Which, the company says, has “over 800 fully completed construction contracts valued from $10,000 to $40,000,000,” as a subcontractor for companies including Amazon, UPS, FedEx, Starbucks, Coca-Cola, Target, Pepsi, Kraft Heinz, Cargill, Frito-Lay and Jennie-O. Darana Hybrid is an acknowledged expert in building conveyor-type systems used by companies like Amazon to pull products from stock and send them down the line from one step to the next, and the next and the next, and eventually out the door to the customers. Brandon Dill/The Washington Post/Getty Images In Darana Hybrid, Musk found a lean, fast-moving contractor to handle construction of his latest projects in Memphis and its Southaven suburb. And Cuttell responded in kind, dropping $10.5 million on a 169,000-square-foot industrial building located near Musk’s pet projects, to house Darana Hybrid equipment needed to work for Musk. That first project, Colossus, went online in Memphis in mid-2024, not long before Cuttell became deeply interested in the IHRA. Called “the world’s largest supercomputer,” Colossus is essentially a giant data center, but not one built out in the open, which typically draws community criticism and often downright outrage because of energy, noise, and environmental concerns. Colossus was constructed inside a massive, long-shuttered factory once used by Electrolux to make vacuum cleaners and Frigidaire appliances. Brilliant, really. Plus, Darana Hybrid knows its way around Memphis, as it was based there before its move to Ohio, and Cuttell himself used to be a resident. Regarded as a “midsized” contractor, there was an element of surprise within the data center world when Darana began applying for big work permits on the project. “A data center industry veteran who reviewed the permit applications said it’s unusual for a smaller company like Darana Hybrid to handle a project of Colossus’ scale,” reported one data-savvy website a year ago. In January, when he appeared in Memphis to announce his purchase of the moribund Memphis Motorsports Park, Cuttell visited St. Jude Children’s Research Hospital and gave the administrators a check for $10 million. He said there would be more. Facebook/IHRA Brandon Dill/The Washington Post/Getty Images Although there is no question that plenty of proposed data farms are getting immense pushback from both politicians and residents, that’s not Musk’s style. In Memphis, he found a city eager to attract high-tech investors. Then he found that 750,000-square-foot vacuum cleaner factory that had been sitting empty since 2022, even though the LEED-certified building had opened just 12 years earlier. Who else would need 750,000 square feet? It was perfect for an unobtrusive, nicely concealed data center. And Musk looks like a local hero for repurposing a legitimately unsellable building and populating it with new employees. And to complete that project in 122 days, or 123, by Cuttell’s reckoning, is remarkable by any measure. Darana Hybrid’s work for Elon Musk and Space xAI should have been enough to ensure a busy, high-profile future for Darana Hybrid, a company that Cuttell started himself, working alongside his seven employees. According to the website Datanyze , Darana Hybrid now employs 379. But as Cuttell told the Daily Memphian last week, had he known this crisis was coming, “I would have demanded more money up front. But we were in such a big rush to get this job done,” he said. “I never got a thank you or nothing for pulling one off in six weeks. I mean, that’s super dirty.” Brandon Dill/The Washington Post/Getty Images Where’s the Money? Even if Darryl Cuttell does get the $600 million he claims that Elon Musk owes him, why did he spend so heavily on the International Hot Rod Association? And all the tracks and series he acquired, or tried to? He had to know the odds of making a dime were slim. I asked Cuttell that question at the 2025 PRI trade show, and he said it was because he wanted to make it “fair for the racer, for the little guy. He isn’t getting that now.” Without naming the NHRA, he was effectively naming the NHRA. That was all he’d say; it was Leah Martin or longtime broadcaster Ralph Sheheen who did the talking at press conferences that weekend. Never Cuttell. Facebook/IHRA Fast-forward to last spring. The money ran out, and apparently there was no one to tell Cuttell, “ Enough, already.” Indeed, the IHRA had been ripe for a revival. Had Cuttell invested in the series conservatively, and concentrated only on drag racing, that money might have lasted a lot longer, and perhaps could have provided a solid foundation. But as one drag racing insider, who had a very close look inside Cuttell’s IHRA, guessed at what happened: “Darryll wasn’t just spending money he had made from Elon Musk, he spent money he thought he would be making from Elon Musk.” So the IHRA is effectively done. Again. There’s nothing left. So many people and companies have not been paid, including the racers who won in that first and only Triple Crown event. Tracks have not been paid. Emergency workers and concessionaires, most all of which fronted the money it took to get to the races and stay for the duration, are out that investment. At last word, the production company that provided the free, high-quality live digital feed of the major races hasn’t been made whole and is owed well into six figures. Even some of the companies that rented Cuttell the mandatory Ferris wheels that spun lazily over every major IHRA event are left standing in line. Will everybody get paid? Richard Freeman said that based on his conversations with Cuttell, the odds seem long. Cuttell might be lucky, Freeman said, to just get out of this mess and remain a free man. Facebook/IHRA Many of the IHRA racers who planned their season by what they expected to earn by competing in the IHRA, spent money on their cars, shops, and equipment, based on what they were told by the sanctioning body. Either because they are limited geographically, or because the IHRA’s rules and competition classes differ from the NHRA’s, a substantial number of racers now have no place to race. There’s already a plethora of drag cars being offered for sale online and elsewhere, and seldom at a profit. Alan Reinhart, the 30-year NHRA employee who jumped to the IHRA and then was gone a week after I interviewed him, finally made his true opinion of Cuttell and the IHRA known in an online post. “I do believe that Darryl went into this with the intention of it being Great! Then instead of listening to experts that he hired, listened to morons who knew nothing about how to make this work. Congrats to those guys, it was you, not us, that cost Darryl a few hundred million dollars and left this mess for the racers who believed.” But none of that answers that question for Cuttell—what did he see in the IHRA that led him to spend that “few hundred million dollars” on the series? Leah Martin had been named president just five weeks earlier when she gave an interview to speedonthewater.com, and journalist Matt Trulio asked that question. Here’s what Martin said: “For his legacy. He’s never been married. He’s never had children. So he feels like this is his legacy. He loves racing. He loves speed. Darryl sees this as his legacy.” Facebook/IHRA Well, not this perhaps. This will take a long time to reconcile. Is this the last chapter in the IHRA’s 56-year history? I asked Grok, Elon Musk’s online bot that researches questions and answers them, “What will happen to the IHRA?” Grok said, “The International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA) remains stable and operational.” Perhaps I should be more specific. “What will happen to the IHRA racing series?” Grok thought for another 20 seconds, possibly with the help of Colossus in Memphis that Musk and Cuttell built, and came back with this: “The International Hot Rod Association (IHRA) is in significant turmoil in mid-2026 under owner/CEO Darryl Cuttell (who acquired it in late 2024). Professional/national series have been largely canceled or heavily cut for the rest of 2026 amid budget shortfalls, facility issues, staff cuts/layoffs, and reported payment problems, with a stated shift toward grassroots programs and a planned ‘reset’ for 2027. Ownership status is unclear amid sale rumors, and the long-term future remains uncertain.” Aside from being a bit optimistic, Grok’s sketchy guess sounds as good as anyone’s. The post How Darryl Cuttell’s Would-Be IHRA Empire Came Crashing Down appeared first on Hagerty Media .

Beyond Next-Token Prediction: A Performance Characterization of Diffusion versus Autoregressive Language Models
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved state-of-the-art performance on a broad range of Natural Language Processing (NLP) tasks…
body_text: View publication Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved state-of-the-art performance on a broad range of Natural Language Processing (NLP) tasks, including document processing and code generation. Autoregressive Language Models (ARMs), which generate tokens sequentially conditioned on all previous tokens, have been the predominant paradigm for LLMs. While these models have achieved high accuracy across a range of downstream tasks, they exhibit low arithmetic intensity due to the inherent sequential dependency in next-token prediction. Recently, Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) have emerged as a promising alternative architecture. DLMs generate output tokens in parallel, mitigating the limitations of sequential decoding. However, the performance implications of DLMs relative to commonly deployed ARMs are not fully understood. In this work, we present a comprehensive study of the performance characteristics of ARMs and DLMs, combining theoretical analysis with empirical profiling to characterize the trade-offs between these approaches. We show that although DLMs can achieve higher arithmetic intensity than ARMs by leveraging parallelism across token positions, they fail to scale effectively with longer contexts. We then explore block-wise decoding for DLMs, which decouples arithmetic intensity from sequence length and enables better scaling to long contexts (similar to ARMs). We also examine batched inference and find that ARMs exhibit superior throughput as they benefit more from parallelism across sequences in the batch. Finally, we highlight opportunities for accelerating DLM inference, emphasizing that reducing the number of sampling steps is key for open-source DLMs to achieve lower latency relative to ARMs. † Seoul National University ‡ University of California, Berkeley § ICSI ¶ LBNL †† University of Texas at Austin * Advisory role

title: Formance vs Fragment: Built for What Comes After the MVP
summary: Compare Formance vs Fragment for post-MVP ledger scale across programmable logic, multi-asset support, reconciliation, deployment, and auditability.
body_text: Teams comparing Formance vs Fragment need to know whether the system of record built for the MVP still holds as transaction volume rises and regulatory obligations spread across more payment rails. Your first chart of accounts took an afternoon to model at MVP stage. Eighteen months later, the same ledger sits under a dozen payment providers. It also supports a stablecoin leg the product team added last quarter and a safeguarding audit on the calendar. The MVP-era ledger is now the post-MVP bottleneck, and two systems answer that question differently. Formance is an open-source, programmable core ledger that unifies fiat and digital assets with regulatory-grade traceability, built for what comes after the MVP. Fragment is a managed ledger API often evaluated by teams trying to reach a correct double-entry model quickly at the MVP stage. They are built for different phases of the same company. What is an MVP ledger? An MVP (Minimum Viable Product) is the earliest shippable version of a product. It is the smallest feature set that lets a team validate the core value proposition with real users. In ledger terms, an MVP ledger is the first pass at a financial system of record, typically a single-currency, single-rail, double-entry model that supports one or two payment providers and a handful of account types. It's optimized for speed to first transaction, but it breaks down against the multi-rail, multi-asset, multi-jurisdiction reality that emerges once the product gains traction. Post-MVP is the phase where that initial model meets production volume, new payment rails, additional asset classes, and regulatory obligations it was never designed to carry. Why Formance works post-MVP Formance puts the logic inside the ledger, keeps it programmable, and makes correctness a property of the ledger itself. At the post-MVP scale, financial logic that lives outside the ledger becomes middleware that must be written, tested, and maintained forever. Formance offers teams the financial logic, correctness guarantees, and an audit trail within the ledger itself, so multi-party postings, fee splits, and reserve movements remain programmable and provable without a layer of middleware to maintain them. Formance's programmable logic inside the ledger The Formance Ledger executes multi-party postings, fee splits, reserve movements, and fund-attribution logic as first-class ledger operations. The ledger becomes the single source of financial truth. The core is MIT-licensed with full source on GitHub, and it's available as Open Source / Community Edition, Enterprise Self-Hosted, or Enterprise Private Cloud. Financial figures can be described in Numscript, Formance's purpose-built language for describing financial transactions. A multi-party settlement that would otherwise be backend code wrapped in transaction handling and retry logic becomes a handful of send statements that both engineers and finance teams can read without translation. When the fee structure changes, the change is shipped as a script edit, and the intent remains auditable in one place. Formance's structural correctness The Formance Ledger enforces correctness at write time. It records ledger postings as append-only entries in a hash-chained transaction history that is never rewritten. It tracks both recorded and effective time for each transaction, so engineers can backdate corrections and reconstruct any balance at any historical point. When a transaction affects multiple accounts, it either commits in full or not at all. Formance blocks unbalanced writes and commits multi-account transactions atomically. An unbalanced transaction cannot commit, so orphan value is structurally impossible. Atomic multi-posting means that a transaction affecting many accounts succeeds or fails as a single unit. Complex split-and-fee logic and reserve movements stay consistent inside the ledger. At low volume, these properties read like bonuses. Under regulatory scrutiny, they are prerequisites. A Numscript example in practice A merchant pays a recipient $5,000 from its omnibus account , the platform captures a 2% fee, and a parallel 2,500 USDC leg settles to the same recipient. The merchant's omnibus account holds both fiat and USDC balances. In Numscript, the entire flow is a single atomic transaction. The accounts are: Real-world party Ledger account Holds Merchant @merchants:acme:omnibus the merchant's USD and USDC balance Recipient @users:alice:wallet the recipient's received USD and USDC Platform fee income @platform:revenue:fees platform fee revenue The merchant disburses $5,000.00. Of the USD leg, 2% goes to platform fee revenue, and the remainder goes to the recipient. The 2,500 USDC leg goes to the same recipient. // MERCHANT_DISBURSEMENT // Event: merchant disburses USD and USDC; platform keeps a 2% USD fee send [USD/2 500000] ( source = @merchants:acme:omnibus destination = { 2 % to @platform:revenue:fees remaining to @users:alice:wallet } ) send [USDC/6 2500000000] ( source = @merchants:acme:omnibus destination = @users:alice:wallet ) set_tx_meta ( "event_type" , "merchant_disbursement" ) set_tx_meta ( "disbursement_id" , "dsb001" ) Multiple send statements in one script commit as a single transaction. Execution is atomic, ensuring that either all modeled transactions are committed, or none are. The fiat leg and the stablecoin leg cannot diverge. Around a prescriptive ledger API, teams typically open a database transaction, lock the omnibus balance, compute the fee, insert postings for the fiat leg, call a separate path for the stablecoin leg, handle the case where the first succeeds and the second times out, attach a deduplication key so the webhook retry doesn't run everything twice, and emit audit records. Every step is code that your team writes, tests, and maintains, and the transaction's intent is scattered across services rather than stated in a single script. Formance's auditable, point-in-time history Every posting is auditable and reconstructable to any past moment. The hash chain makes the history tamper-evident, and the transaction remains readable by a finance analyst without an engineering ticket to interpret it. Adding another ledger leg or asset movement is another send statement inside the same atomic transaction. Formance Ledger supports point-in-time views and backdated corrections without rewriting history, thanks to its bi-temporal model. Middleware-based logic often reaches the same outcome only by reprocessing history and reconciling by hand. When post-MVP ledger complexity catches up MVP-era financial logic degrades quietly, then expensively. Each new provider adds a data format and a settlement-timing quirk, while each reconciliation failure gets patched with a script. Then, each patch adds hours to month-end close. The Liberis situation shows the pattern in real life. Bundled transactions and split mechanisms among multiple partners made reconciliation difficult to manage as their program expanded, and their engineering team spent time building basic ledger functionality instead of shipping product. Formance reports Liberis achieved zero reconciliation errors across 14 countries over 1.5 years in production. Four trigger events tend to force the architecture conversation: 1 A regulation deadline: For example, the FCA's PS25/12 rules, in force since 7 May 2026, require daily reconciliation of safeguarded funds, annual safeguarding audits, and monthly regulatory returns for UK payment firms. Similar pressure is landing from MiCA , DORA , and the GENIUS Act , each of which pushes data integrity, reconciliation, and reserve disclosure requirements directly into ledger architecture. 2 Payment rail splits: Providers multiply past what the original model assumed, and every added statement format and cut-off behavior lands on a schema designed for two. 3 Automated reconciliation as an engineering tax: Manual matching scripts break whenever a provider changes formats and consume hours that were budgeted for features. 4 A poorly constructed balance execution: A balance nobody can explain, or a duplicate posting after a network retry. Any of these triggers on their own is manageable. Stacked together, they force a choice about where financial logic lives: either inside a ledger built to carry it, or spread across middleware that must be maintained forever. That choice is where Formance and Fragment diverge, and it's easier to see by starting with the case Fragment was built for. Why Fragment works at MVP stage Fragment is built for teams that want to reach a correct double-entry ledger fast without owning ledger infrastructure at the MVP stage. The trade-offs (closed source, cloud-only deployment, and customization limits as flows grow) are acceptable when the product is single-asset, single-rail, and not yet under regulatory pressure. Fragment's schema-first managed platform Accounts and entry patterns are declared through a schema, and Fragment generates the tooling around them. The visual ledger simulator is a genuine evaluation-stage advantage for teams that want to model accounts and simulate entries quickly, and the declared structure can be attractive before production buildout. For a narrow, well-understood use case, onboarding may be fast, and the developer experience can be strong. The fit becomes shakier when a new payment rail or market requires an asset class or logic the initial model does not comfortably express. If custom transaction logic is not expressed within the ledger core, multi-step coordination must live around the ledger. As flows grow into multi-party settlements or non-standard business logic, customization tends to shift from inside the platform to code written around it. Fragment's evaluation-stage advantage Fragment's main appeal is getting to a financially correct balance infrastructure quickly. The simulator-led workflow is useful for teams that want to model accounts and simulate entries before writing production code, and the guided schema-first modeling approach is helpful. Stripe's backing gives it credibility, and its standard debit/credit model is immediately familiar to finance teams. Commercial fit is a separate question, and teams should confirm current pricing directly and whether the managed model fits their operating requirements. Fragment's fit for early-stage teams Without a dedicated infrastructure engineer, a tightly managed, bounded cloud ledger is a rational choice. Fragment fits a narrow single-asset, single-rail flow with minimal regulatory requirements and no multi-rail, multi-entity, or multi-market planned expansion. Fragment's trade-offs at scale Vendor-controlled architecture makes deployment flexibility and structural changes open questions once new rails or asset classes arrive under regulator scrutiny. Migrating a core ledger is open-heart surgery. Formance vs Fragment feature comparison Formance and Fragment differ on source access, deployment, customization, reconciliation, and compliance posture as payment rails, assets, and compliance requirements grow: Property Formance Fragment License and source access MIT-licensed core ledger with full source available Closed source, and no code inspection Multi-asset support Fiat and digital assets tracked natively, with balances and precision maintained per asset Single-asset model per entry; multi-asset flows require coordination in application code Transaction language Numscript DSL and logic executes inside the ledger Schema-driven entry model, but customization narrows as flows grow more complex API surface REST API with atomic multi-posting support. Numscript is executed server-side Managed API, but integration and debugging depth vary by use case Connectivity Pre-built connectors (Stripe, Adyen, Wise, Fireblocks, and others) plus a generic connector framework Custom ingestion and provider workflow requirements may require code around the ledger Reconciliation Drift detection and balance verification against external provider records No deep audit or traceability tooling Orchestration Flows offers event-driven multi-step workflows No orchestration engine because custom multi-step logic lives around the ledger Deployment Open Source / Community Edition, Enterprise Self-Hosted, or Enterprise Private Cloud Cloud-hosted only with no self-hosting or data residency control Certifications SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001 certified, DORA-assessed, and MiCA and GENIUS alignment Early-stage product with limited enterprise track record and unclear compliance posture Formance vs Fragment: which ledger fits your MVP stage? The choice between Formance and Fragment comes down to where your product sits on the MVP-to-post-MVP curve, including your stage, your regulatory surface area, and how much of your product's financial logic you're willing to maintain as middleware around the ledger. Formance's Ledger when you're past MVP and the ledger has to carry real weight Choose Formance if you are Series A or later with multi-rail or multi-asset flows across fiat and digital assets , a regulated entity carrying EMI, MTL, MiCA, or DORA obligations, a company that needs self-hosted deployment for data sovereignty, or a team whose product logic is complex enough that encoding it inside the ledger beats maintaining it as middleware. Formance is built for what comes after the MVP: programmable, auditable, and yours to run wherever your compliance posture demands. Fragment is ideal when you're at the MVP stage and speed is the only thing that matters Choose Fragment if you are early-stage with a single-asset, single-rail product, no near-term regulatory exposure, no multi-market plans in the early stages, and no engineering bandwidth to run infrastructure at the component level. Fragment's guided modeling workflow and managed developer experience can get you to a correct double-entry ledger quickly. Confirm current pricing and evaluation terms directly before committing.

title: Remittance Advice: The Missing Link Between Payment and Reconciliation
summary: Learn what remittance advice contains, how it differs from a payment confirmation, and why structured data improves invoice matching.
body_text: Remittance advice is information a payer sends to explain what a payment covers. It may identify one invoice, several invoices, credit adjustments, tax amounts, discounts, or a partial payment. The payment moves funds. The remittance advice tells the recipient how to apply them. Without that context, accounts receivable teams may receive the correct amount and still spend hours determining which open records to close. The problem becomes more common when one payment settles several invoices or when fees and deductions make the received amount differ from the invoice total. Remittance advice is not a payment confirmation A payment confirmation proves that an instruction was submitted, accepted, or completed, depending on the system. Remittance advice describes the commercial records associated with the payment. Payment instruction: What money should move, where, and when? Payment status: Was the instruction accepted, settled, returned, or failed? Remittance advice: Which invoices, credits, or obligations does the payment cover? ERP posting: How should the event affect the books? One message may contain more than one of these elements, but product teams should preserve the distinctions. A successful payment without usable remittance data can still create a cash-application exception. What remittance advice should contain Useful remittance data depends on the use case. Common fields include payer and payee identifiers, payment reference, invoice number, invoice date, original amount, amount paid, currency, discounts, credits, tax details, and free-text notes. Stable identifiers are more reliable than text. "April invoices" may be readable to a person and difficult to match. An invoice ID, end-to-end payment ID, and customer account identifier create a stronger join across systems. ISO 20022 treats remittance as structured payment information. Its remittance advice message definition allows an originator to provide details associated with a payment, including invoice line information. Remittance can travel with the payment or separately, as long as the recipient can reliably associate the two. Why ERP context matters ERP records contain the invoices, customers, bills, vendors, credits, and accounts the payment needs to resolve. When remittance information reaches the ERP with stable identifiers, a system can propose or complete a match and retain the evidence beside the accounting entry. Problems arise when the data is truncated, reformatted, or stored only in a bank portal. A bank statement description may preserve a payer name and short reference while losing the invoice-level breakdown. An emailed PDF may contain the detail but remain disconnected from the transaction. Rutter's Accounting API gives fintech products read and write access to invoices, bills, payments, and related ERP records. Rutter's Bank Feeds deliver transaction data into accounting systems. A complete reconciliation product needs a reliable way to associate the transaction with the relevant remittance and ERP records. One payment may settle many invoices Batch settlement is where remittance advice earns its keep. Suppose a customer sends $48,500 against five invoices totaling $50,000 and applies a $1,500 credit. Amount matching alone sees a discrepancy. Structured remittance can explain the five allocations and the credit. Partial payments create a related case. Advice should identify the invoice and amount paid without marking the entire receivable as settled. Overpayments may create a customer credit or unresolved balance depending on policy. Nacha's ACH file details show how addenda records can carry payment-related information for certain ACH uses. Available space and conventions vary, so product teams should test what survives through every bank, rail, and ERP involved in the flow. Design for separation and reassociation Remittance advice sometimes arrives before the payment, after it, or through a different channel. The system needs an identifier that allows the records to reunite. Good candidates include a payment ID, end-to-end ID, customer reference, or another unique value agreed across the workflow. Avoid matching on amount and date alone when the payment volume makes collisions plausible. Payer identity and currency help. Invoice references provide stronger evidence. Confidence should determine whether the product auto-applies the payment or proposes a match for review. Corrections need their own path. A payer may send revised advice after noticing a misapplied invoice. The recipient should be able to update the allocation without losing the original message or bank transaction. Embedded reconciliation puts the evidence together An ERP-native workflow can show the transaction, remittance details, candidate invoices, credits, and final accounting result in one place. Rutter Embedded ERP supports banking, payment, and reconciliation experiences inside supported ERPs while banks and fintechs retain their own financial rails. A related guide explains how automated reconciliation turns that context into matched records and reviewable exceptions. Rutter's article on embedded reconciliation infrastructure focuses on getting transaction data into the accounting system. Remittance advice is the context layer that can make that transaction easier to apply once it arrives. What product teams should test Test one-to-one, one-to-many, partial, overpaid, short-paid, credited, refunded, fee-adjusted, and foreign-currency scenarios. Confirm maximum field lengths and character handling on every rail. Check whether structured fields survive aggregator and bank transformations. Verify that late or corrected advice can be reassociated without duplicating the payment. Track unapplied cash, automatic-match rate, time to apply, corrections, and remittance completeness. Those measures show whether the feature closes work or merely transports another document. Remittance advice looks secondary because it does not move money. For finance teams trying to reconcile at scale, it carries the explanation that turns movement into an accounting event.

title: Choosing the Right Steel Drum: Why Size Matters
summary: The 55-gallon (~220 liter) steel drum is about as close to a universal standard as industrial packaging gets. It shows up in chemical plants, food and
body_text: The 55-gallon (~220 liter) steel drum is about as close to a universal standard as industrial packaging gets. It shows up in chemical plants, food and beverage lines, lubricant blending, anywhere bulk liquids need to move. For a lot of applications, it’s still the right call. But what if your product doesn’t need that much room? Shipping a partially filled 220L drum means paying to move empty space, plus higher freight costs and more packaging than the job requires. Whether you’re filling specialty chemicals, food ingredients, laboratory reagents, or high-value formulations, matching drum size to actual volume tightens up your supply chain instead of just filling a container. A drum that’s too large can mean: Paying to transport unused capacity Higher packaging material consumption More storage space required More product residue left behind after dispensing While a drum that’s too small cuts the other way: more containers, more handling time, more labor, and even more shipping runs. Matching the drum to the product is what keeps operations lean either direction. A Wide Range of Sizes, Built to the Same Standard Greif’s small and intermediate steel drums span 15L to 160L, open head or tight head, giving manufacturers real flexibility instead of rounding up to the nearest standard size. That covers laboratory chemicals and specialty coatings at the small end, lubricants and food ingredients in the middle, and larger intermediates near the top. Smaller doesn’t mean lighter-duty. These drums are built to the same quality standards as Greif’s full-size steel drums, with the same durability and reliable protection through storage and transport. Depending on the application, they’re available with removable tops for easier filling and cleaning, or tight-head configurations for secure liquid transport, and with the same internal lining options as Greif’s larger drums. Why Manufacturers Choose Greif Greif offers one of the industry’s broadest ranges, from small sizes to the standard 220L drum, so manufacturers can scale production without switching suppliers or compromising quality. As production needs shift, having every size available from one trusted supplier simplifies procurement and keeps operations running smoothly. title: Five business advantages that hinge on your QA strategy
summary: Quality assurance does more than catch defects — it drives business value. Read our latest blog post for five business advantages that hinge on your QA strategy.
body_text: Most organizations have quality assurance. Fewer have quality assurance that actively drives business value. The difference lies in where it sits and how seriously it’s treated as a strategic capability rather than a final-stage filter. Quality assurance (QA) is part of an organization’s overall governance process. It involves testing development code and assuring it’s been built to the required specifications. It’s a critical step in the application life cycle. It enables an organization to detect and fix defects before the final application or feature release, when they are far more costly to resolve. Embedding quality earlier in the development life cycle can reduce costly rework and improve release outcomes before issues reach customers. Enterprises want faster releases, better customer experiences, improved operational resilience, and greater engineering productivity However, many still treat quality assurance as a downstream checkpoint, a function that catches defects rather than prevents them. This disconnect is a strategic blind spot. Closing it opens five meaningful business advantages. #1: Protect your brand reputation When customers use your applications, they expect a seamless, user-friendly experience. If they experience software defects or difficulty navigating its capabilities, they’re less likely to use it and may seek alternatives. The same applies to employees' expectations of internal applications. Upstream QA catches customer-facing defects before they can impact users and potentially harm your organization’s brand reputation. Reliable applications strengthen customer trust and loyalty. #2: Minimize costly rework Organizations commit a set number of hours to developers, project managers, testers, and other employees involved in application development. Quality failures require costly, unanticipated rework from these team members and the reallocation of budget previously earmarked for other spending. When QA is embedded earlier in the development cycle and supported by continuous, automated testing, releases go more smoothly and your organization’s developers can spend time working on new capabilities and new applications. This can mean more opportunities to profit, attracting new customers, and gaining additional traction with existing customers. #3: Avoid productivity and operational disruptions Multiple team members are invested in releasing high-quality applications. Software issues disrupt operations and cause churn by forcing employees to redo work, pulling them away from other tasks. Additional people may even need to be pulled in to work on a fix. This decreases overall productivity. Teams with QA embedded earlier in the development process benefit from more stable releases, increasing employee productivity and keeping operations running smoothly. This minimizes operational and productivity disruptions and delays, so you can keep innovating and achieving your business objectives. #4: Accelerate time-to-market Unstable releases, those that slip through testing with undiscovered defects, undermine an organization’s ability to overcome the pressures of market competition. If competitors have stronger quality assurance practices, their applications might be more reliable and more attractive to consumers who prioritize reliability. Organizations with mature QA practices, increasingly powered by AI-driven and automated testing, can accelerate time-to-market without compromising the commitment to deliver on schedule. A well-executed quality assurance process helps ensure the product matches expectations within the promised timeframe, increasing customer confidence. #5: Build digital resilience Digital resilience separates market leaders from followers because the former don’t compromise on the quality of their applications . They recognize that delivering high-quality applications helps them stay agile and able to adapt and recover when the unexpected occurs. Strategic QA protects your digital ecosystem by identifying defects and security vulnerabilities early and ensuring seamless performance before issues ripple through your business. If the unexpected happens, such as a spike in users or an emerging security threat, your systems stay responsive and reliable. Consider the business benefits of quality assurance Quality assurance clearly matters. The real question is whether yours is positioned to drive business value or whether it’s still treated as a checkpoint at the end of the line. As automation, autonomous systems, and agentic AI grow, QA must evolve alongside them. That means building quality in earlier, resourcing it properly, and measuring it against business outcomes, such as release velocity, operational stability, customer satisfaction, and resilience.
